result:
The proposed answer n − 1 is very likely incorrect, because both halves of the argument have gaps.

**Upper bound.** The solution only shows that the space V of admissible polynomials has dimension at least 2. It then claims that a generic element of V avoids every non-edge condition. That holds only if no non-edge hyperplane contains all of V, and this is never checked. The argument also does not rule out a much smaller degree working.

**Lower bound.** The general-n construction is not justified. The listed coefficients b, c, d, e, f are never defined, and the claim that P(z₁, zₙ) = 0 on all of V is only asserted. The proof works only for n = 3 and the n = 4 case it sketches.

**Dimension count.** A polynomial of degree at most k has (k+1)(k+2)/2 coefficients. The edge conditions impose 2(n−1) linear constraints, because both orders (zᵢ, zⱼ) and (zⱼ, zᵢ) must vanish. A nonzero solution therefore needs roughly (k+1)(k+2)/2 > 2(n−1), which means k grows like 2√n. That is far below n − 1 for large n, so n − 1 cannot be the minimum in general. For example, n = 100 would give a degree around 20 instead of 99.

The values n = 3 and n = 4 agree with n − 1 only by coincidence of small cases. I recall the true answer being of the form about ⌈2√(n−1)⌉, but I did not derive it here.

VERDICT: REJECT
